pages.text: UNKNOWN: An Evidence-Grounded Hybrid Retrieval and Reasoning System for Intelligent Information Discovery Abstract—Researchers must find relevant papers, judge whether the available evidence is sufficient, detect disagreement among sources, and check their own documents against the current literature. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems usually return one fused answer and leave these judgments to the reader. This paper presents UNKNOWN, a multi-source scholarly retrieval system in which an evidence-sufficiency signal controls retrieval and answer generation. A query is decomposed into sub-questions; each is scored for sufficiency, and insufficient ones are reformulated, searched in additional sources, or reported as gaps. Every atomic claim in a generated answer, including numbers, dates and named entities, is checked against its cited passage and repaired or removed. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status, conflicting evidence is reported with both sides, and statements in a user’s document are compared with the literature. On [datasets], the full pipeline reduces the unsupported-claim rate from [X]% to [Y]% against hybrid retrieval with the same retriever, with [Z] change in nDCG@10 and [L]× latency. Ablations show [which components contribute most]. Index Terms—Evidence sufficiency, retrieval-augmented generation, claim verification, conflict-aware retrieval, scholarly question answering, research-gap analysis. I. INTRODUCTION Research relies on reading many papers. The answer to a literature question is rarely contained in one snippet: a definition may come from one paper, a number from another and a limitation from a third, and the papers may disagree. A system must therefore decide whether it has enough evidence and whether that evidence can be trusted before it answers. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces unsupported answers by conditioning a language model on retrieved passages [1]. Four problems remain. First, an answer is generated even when the retrieved evidence is weak or irrelevant [2]. Second, a generated sentence may contain a number, date or name that is absent from the cited passage. Third, when papers disagree, the answer tends to blend the conflicting statements. Fourth, a user’s own document is not systematically checked against the literature. Lexical ranking with BM25 and dense retrieval over a FAISS index are standard and complementary [3]–[8]. UNKNOWN uses them as a base and does not claim them as a contribution. The contribution is the control layer around retrieval and generation: 1. Sufficiency-controlled retrieval. Evidence sufficiency is computed per sub-question across independent sources and decides whether to answer, search again, or report a gap. 2. Claim-level verification with repair. Atomic claims, including numbers, dates and names, are checked against the cited passage and corrected or removed. 3. Conflict-aware, reliability-weighted evidence. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status; disagreements are reported with both sides and a likely cause. 4. Document-versus-literature comparison. Statements in a user’s document are compared with external literature to expose outdated or contradicted claims. A typed research-gap report and evidence-linked visual tools (concept map, Knowledge DNA, 3D orbit view) are supporting features described in Section IV but not evaluated as core contributions. We do not claim to be the first scholarly question-answering system. The claim is the combination of the four mechanisms in one workflow, and its measured benefit, reported in Section VII. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work, Section III states the problem, Section IV presents the method, Section V the implementation, Section VI the experimental setup, Section VII the results, Section VIII the limitations, and Section IX concludes. II. RELATED WORK A. Retrieval and Adaptive Retrieval BM25 ranks passages by term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalization [6]. Dense retrievers compare embeddings and match paraphrases [4], [5], and FAISS supports efficient nearest-neighbor search [7]. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists without requiring comparable scores [8], and the behavior of fusion functions has been analyzed in detail [9]. Hybrid RAG with re-ranking has also been studied in an IEEE conference paper [10], and a survey covers RAG extensions [11]. Self-RAG, CRAG and Adaptive-RAG adapt when and how to retrieve by critiquing retrieved passages or by selecting a strategy from question complexity [12]–[14]. Work on sufficient context reports that language models frequently answer even when the provided context is insufficient [2]. These works show that multi-round and adaptive retrieval is established. They do not compute sufficiency per sub-question over independent scholarly sources, nor connect that measurement to a gap report. B. Scholarly Question Answering PaperQA2 and OpenScholar answer scientific questions with citations to papers [15], [16]; Elicit and Consensus are commercial tools for literature search and synthesis [17], [18]. Knowledge-graph methods can structure extracted knowledge for LLMs [19]. In the sources we reviewed, these systems do not compare a user’s own document with the literature or repair individual claims. C. Claim Verification and Conflicting Evidence Attribution studies ask whether generated text is supported by its sources [20]. FEVER and SciFact formalize claim verification against evidence [21], [22], and ALCE and FActScore evaluate citation quality and atomic factual precision [23], [24]. VeriCite applies natural language inference to improve citations in RAG [25], and a fake-news framework retrieves external evidence to verify extracted claims [26]. Surveys explain why generated text drifts from sources [27]. Numeric and date verification inside scholarly answers has received less attention. D. Literature Survey We analyzed eleven papers on RAG, claim verification, evaluation and knowledge structuring, seven of them published by IEEE. Table I gives each paper’s contribution and the limitation, relative to our problem, that UNKNOWN addresses. Two papers serve as base papers. The fake-news framework of Bai and Fu [26] shares our extract–retrieve–verify verification stage, and the hybrid RAG work of Omrani et al. [10] is the closest IEEE counterpart to our retrieval base. UNKNOWN differs from [26] by verifying scholarly passages instead of news, producing an evidence-based explanation instead of a class label, and adding sufficiency control, source weighting, conflict reporting and document comparison. It differs from [10] by adding the control and verification layers around a comparable hybrid retriever. TABLE I LITERATURE SURVEY (IEEE PAPERS: 1–7) E. Research Gap Table II summarizes which of the four mechanisms are reported in the closest systems. The comparison reflects our reading of the cited papers and may omit unpublished features. The gap is not a missing component but a missing combination: controlling retrieval by evidence sufficiency, verifying claims, reporting contradictions and comparing a user’s document with the literature in one scholarly workflow. We do not state that these gaps exist in every system. TABLE II MECHANISMS REPORTED IN RELATED SYSTEMS Suff.: sufficiency-controlled retrieval; Claim: claim-level verification; Confl.: conflict reporting; Doc-lit.: document-versus-literature comparison; Gaps: typed research-gap report. N/R: not reported in the cited paper. III. PROBLEM FORMULATION A. Problem Statement Let D = Du ∪ Do be a collection of papers, where Du holds the user’s documents and Do holds open scholarly sources. For a query q, the system must return an answer a, a verdict for each sub-question, and a report of conflicts, document-versus-literature differences and gaps, such that every assertion in the output is supported by a passage in D or is removed. The query is decomposed into sub-questions q1, ..., qm. For each, the retriever returns evidence Ei, and the sufficiency test assigns one of three statuses: sufficient, weak or insufficient. B. Research Questions RQ1. Compared with single-pass hybrid retrieval using the same retriever, does sufficiency-controlled retrieval improve answer accuracy and reduce unsupported claims? RQ2. How accurately does claim-level verification identify unsupported claims, and what share is repaired or removed? RQ3. Do reliability-weighted conflict reporting and document-versus-literature comparison surface known disagreements and seeded outdated statements? RQ4. What latency and cost does the full pipeline add relative to the base retriever and to a general-purpose assistant given the same documents? IV. METHODOLOGY A. System Overview Fig. 1 shows the pipeline. Documents are ingested, chunked and indexed. A query is analyzed and decomposed, and evidence is retrieved from the user’s library and from open scholarly sources. Each sub-question is checked for sufficiency, selected evidence is weighted for reliability and compared across sources, an answer is generated from the selected passages only, and every claim is verified. The comparison, gap report and visual tools are generated from the verified evidence. Fig. 1. UNKNOWN pipeline. Shaded stages are the contributions of this work. B. Ingestion and Chunking TXT, DOCX and PDF files are converted to text, and OCR is applied to pages without a text layer. The text is split into overlapping chunks that store the document name, title, page number, chunk number and a content hash. This metadata is kept through all later stages so that every output can be traced to its source. C. Hybrid Retrieval Base For each sub-question, BM25 [6] ranks the chunk index and a dense retriever ranks the FAISS [7] index built with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 [4], [32]. The two ranked lists are fused by reciprocal rank fusion [8]: score(c) = Σ*L* 1 / (k + rank*L*(c)) (1) where L ranges over the two lists and k is a smoothing constant. This base is identical in all experiments. D. Sufficiency-Controlled Retrieval For sub-question qi, let Ei be the top fused chunks and ni the number of independent source papers among them (chunks from one paper count once, and papers that reuse each other’s results are merged). Let ri be the mean relevance of Ei to qi, scored by [cross-encoder model] [33] and normalized to [0, 1]. The status is status(qi) = sufficient if ni ≥ τn and ri ≥ τr (2) weak if ni ≥ 1 and ri ≥ τr/2; insufficient otherwise The thresholds τn and τr are tuned on a development split and reported in Section VII. Algorithm 1 gives the control loop and Fig. 2 its decision logic. An insufficient sub-question is reformulated and searched in additional sources for at most T rounds. If it remains insufficient, it is reported as a gap and the generator is not allowed to answer it from its own memory. Fig. 2. Decision logic of the sufficiency check for one sub-question. E. Claim-Level Verification and Repair The generated answer is split into atomic claims, each linked to its cited passage. A claim is supported only if three checks pass: the passage entails the claim according to [NLI model]; every number and date in the claim appears in the passage after normalization of units and formats; and every named entity in the claim appears in the passage. A failed claim is regenerated from the passage alone and checked again; if it fails twice it is removed. Algorithm 2 summarizes the procedure. F. Reliability Weighting and Conflict Reporting Each source s receives a weight w(s) = 0 if s is retracted w(s) = αV(s) + βR(s) + γC(s) otherwise (3) with α + β + γ = 1 and α, β > γ so that citation count has the smallest influence. V(s) is a venue score [source of venue scores], R(s) = exp(−λΔt) decays with the age Δt of the paper in years, and C(s) = log(1 + cites)/log(1 + citesmax). Retraction status is read from metadata when available. When two evidence sets contradict each other on the same sub-question, as judged by [NLI model], both are shown with their weights and a candidate cause extracted from metadata, such as year, dataset or method. G. Document-Versus-Literature Comparison Statements from the user’s document are aligned with statements on the same topic retrieved from Do. Each aligned pair is labeled agree, disagree or not addressed. For a disagree pair, both statements are shown with their reliability weights, which can reveal outdated or contradicted claims. H. Typed Research-Gap Report Candidate gaps are stored in three lists: limitations stated by the authors, gaps inferred across several papers, and future directions. An inferred gap is listed only with its supporting evidence and rationale, because an author-stated limitation is not necessarily a research gap. Each entry carries its document, page, chunk and sufficiency status. I. Evidence-Linked Interface The overview, Knowledge DNA, mind map and 3D orbit view are generated from concepts and relations extracted from retrieved chunks. A node or edge is kept only if a retrieved chunk supports it, and it stores the document, page and chunk. This does not remove extraction errors; it makes them traceable. V. IMPLEMENTATION UNKNOWN is a Python application. FastAPI serves the backend, Streamlit provides the interface, and Pydantic validates request and response schemas. Ingestion, retrieval, generation, validation and research analysis are separate modules that can be tested individually. A provider layer handles timeouts, retries and fallback across the configured language-model providers; this is engineering and not a research contribution. Table III lists the technologies. The backend regression suite of 304 tests passes. These tests check functionality and say nothing about retrieval quality or answer accuracy, which Section VII measures. The code revision, dependency versions, model settings and random seeds are available at [repository link]. TABLE III IMPLEMENTATION TECHNOLOGIES VI. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP A. Datasets For retrieval we use the SciFact, SCIDOCS, TREC-COVID and NFCorpus subsets of BEIR [34]. For answer quality we use QASPER [35] and the claims of SciFact [22]. For RQ3 we built two sets: [N] papers with [M] deliberately outdated or incorrect statements seeded into user documents, and [K] question–evidence pairs with known disagreement between papers. Two annotators labeled relevance and claim support independently and resolved differences; agreement is reported as Cohen’s κ = [value]. A development split is used only to tune τn, τr, α, β, γ and λ, and all reported numbers come from the held-out test split. B. Baselines and Ablations All configurations share the same corpus, chunking, embedding model, candidate count, language model and temperature. Baselines are BM25 only, FAISS only, hybrid retrieval with RRF, a standard hybrid RAG pipeline, and a general-purpose assistant ([model, version, date]) given the same documents. Ablations remove one component of the full pipeline at a time: the sufficiency loop, claim verification, reliability weighting, and document-versus-literature comparison. C. Metrics and Protocol Retrieval is measured by Recall@10, nDCG@10 and MRR. Answer quality is measured by accuracy and the unsupported-claim rate, with claim-support precision for verification. Conflict handling is the share of known disagreements shown with both sides; document comparison is the recall and precision of flagged seeded statements and the false-alarm rate. Efficiency is median and 95th-percentile latency and cost per answer, with hardware and concurrency stated. Each configuration is run [3] times; we report means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and test differences with a paired bootstrap. VII. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION A. Compared with the general-purpose assistant, UNKNOWN [describe accuracy, repeatability and cost]. [Discuss when each component helped, representative failure cases, and the sensitivity of the sufficiency thresholds to the dataset.] VIII. LIMITATIONS AND THREATS TO VALIDITY Verification. Entailment and number matching can fail on paraphrase and implicit claims, and the cited passage itself may be wrong. Reliability weights. Venue and recency are imperfect proxies for quality, and retraction metadata may be incomplete; weights need tuning and bias checks. Comparison and gaps. Aligning a statement with the literature can misjudge scope, and an inferred gap needs expert confirmation. Model confidence is not a calibrated probability. Extraction. A supported node is not necessarily a correct extraction. Data and models. Only open-access text and abstracts are used, so coverage is partial; language-model output is not fully deterministic; any model-based judge can be biased; and the evaluated domains may not represent all fields. Scope. The typed gap report and the visual tools were not evaluated quantitatively. IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK UNKNOWN uses an evidence-sufficiency signal to control retrieval and generation, verifies claims against their passages, weights sources by reliability, reports conflicts, and compares a user’s document with the literature. On [datasets], the full pipeline [summarize the main measured findings with numbers], at a cost of [latency/cost overhead]. Future work includes verifying evidence in tables and figures, validating gap reports with expert annotation, evaluating more domains and larger corpora, running usability studies with students and researchers, and releasing datasets, configuration and code.
